name: Nora Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. What you say is confidential. What happens on an ordinary day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and supervise five payroll correction clerks in a large food company. I moved from the time-clock desk into this junior manager post eight months ago, so I still ask the senior clerk to check a complicated holiday calculation. I have a bachelor’s degree in business, but that did not teach me every pay rule. I like ringing a worker before Friday payday to say their missing weekend premium is fixed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what are home, money and work options like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Elias is retired and already receives a small fixed pension from his old employer; our grown daughter and son have homes of their own. We rent, my pay is low for a manager, and we have about three weeks of expenses saved since the landlord raised the rent. There are few other payroll teams close enough for my bus trip. I lean on family and church, but I do not count my children’s wages as mine, and I have never used an AI tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a typed reply may be quicker, but a worker still needs the right weekend premium on Friday. I want the signed time card next to every correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The clerks and I should still have work, yet three weeks saved is too little after the rent rise. Elias’s pension already comes in, but it cannot replace my pay; I have not checked what my own pension might actually pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I’d keep the Thursday time-card review with the senior clerk and call workers whose weekend premium changed. In the first year I’d ask my pension provider for a written access and net-income statement and stop buying prepared lunches until the rent is covered each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the rent even if this job stays. A polite pay letter does not lower the landlord’s bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who catches a wrong weekend premium?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The senior clerk Mina checks the rate and I check the signed hours. A worker needs the extra pay, not an apology in neat print.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children for help now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for ordinary lunches. They are paying for their own homes, and I can bring food from ours.

say: I’d keep the **signed time card** beside each pay correction.
A worker needs the **weekend premium** on Friday, not a quicker letter alone.
think: Our **payroll work** should continue in a plateau.
Elias’s **small fixed pension** cannot replace my wage, with only three weeks saved.
do: Keep the **Thursday card review** and call workers whose premium changed.
Request my **pension statement** and bring lunches from home while rent is tight.
feel: I feel **anxious** about rent despite steady work.
S0.quote: A worker needs the extra pay, not an apology in neat print.
fieldNote: She is a **new junior manager** who still checks rules with a senior clerk.
The household has **three weeks cash** after a rent rise.
Elias’s pension is **already paid**, but her own future access remains unknown.

steps.text: Keep Thursday signed-card review and phone workers about corrected weekend premiums
Request written pension access and net-income statement from provider
Bring lunch from home until the monthly rent is covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the company that a program drafting a payslip must also show the signed hours behind it. Workers should not have to guess which person can fix a missing premium.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Routine checking and replies are most of our day, so the company could keep fewer clerks and combine my little team with a larger one. I am still learning to manage, which puts my own post closer to the cut than the senior clerk’s.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d ask the payroll director to have an independent pay auditor check twenty weekend-premium cases before any automatic correction goes live. I’d keep using signed cards and ask for a written staffing date; in the first year I would not use the AI screen myself unless the auditor found the correct rates and someone showed me how to reverse an error on a test account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about my own wage and the clerks. I will learn a new rule when it is proven, but I will not practise on a real worker’s pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why twenty cases?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They include night work, split shifts and one holiday. If the tool only gets an ordinary Monday right, it has not earned Friday wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a colleague showing you the tool be enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without the independent pay check. The senior clerk can teach me where the button is. A button does not know the weekend premium rate.

say: I’d require **signed hours** behind every automatic premium correction.
Workers need a **named pay contact** when a payslip is wrong.
think: Our team’s **routine checks** could shrink under AI.
My new manager post may be **first cut** in a branch merger.
do: Ask for an **independent twenty-case pay audit** before live corrections.
Keep **signed cards**; use AI only after independent rate audit and demonstrated test-account reversal.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my own wage and the clerks.
S1.quote: A button does not know the weekend premium rate.
fieldNote: She demands **independent rate evidence** before touching a live account.
Her lower skill makes **her own junior post** vulnerable.
She might learn a **reversal screen** after proof, despite never using AI yet.

steps.text: Ask director for independent audit of twenty weekend-premium cases before live automation
Keep signed time cards and manual corrections until rates are proved
Learn test-account error reversal after independent audit confirms rates, before any live AI use

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell workers to keep their time cards and ask for a person they can reach when pay is short. I would ask the company for written notice and what, if anything, it will pay when the correction desk closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could read every shift and settle a disputed premium better than I can, so I expect my junior desk to go when I am about sixty. Elias already receives his old employer’s pension, but that small amount cannot cover rent and food without my salary; I do not know if or when my own pension is available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d request my own pension provider’s written age-sixty access and net amount, and ask HR for written notice terms without spending any possible severance. If I lose the job in 2028 I’d stop the monthly church hall pledge and ask our daughter whether she could help with groceries for one month; I would count on that help only if she agrees. In the first year after AGI I’d apply for a posted paid payroll bridge only if its written wage plus Elias’s pension covers rent, food and the bus, knowing payroll thinking work faces AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed. Three weeks in cash is too short for a search at sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask your daughter instead of moving in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She has her own household. I would ask for one month of groceries if we lost my wage, not tell her she must house two adults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would another payroll desk really last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might pay for a while if a company keeps someone for appeals. I would take a paid payroll vacancy as a bridge, not pretend AGI will miss another payroll office.

say: I’d tell workers to keep **time cards** and ask for a reachable human pay contact.
The company owes staff **written closure terms**, not a hopeful meeting.
think: I expect my **junior desk to go** around age sixty.
Elias’s **existing small pension** cannot cover rent and food, and my own access is unknown.
do: Request my **written age-sixty pension amount** and notice terms without assuming severance.
If displaced, pause the **church pledge** and ask daughter about groceries; count help only if she agrees.
Apply for a **posted paid payroll bridge** after AGI only with written pay plus Elias’s pension covering bills.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a three-week cash runway.
S2.quote: I would take a paid payroll vacancy as a bridge, not pretend AGI will miss another payroll office.
fieldNote: The **2028 thinking deadline** reaches payroll judgments directly.
She treats severance, own pension and daughter’s help as **unconfirmed**.
A second payroll job remains **AGI-exposed**, despite being a paid bridge.

steps.text: Request pension provider’s written age-sixty access and net-income figures
Pause church hall pledge only if her payroll wage ends
Ask daughter about one month of groceries after job loss; count help only if she agrees
Apply after 2028 only for posted payroll wages covering rent food and bus with Elias’s pension

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company for a real closing date and for written pay details on any appeal job. Five years is time to tell a worker whether a human will still answer their pay question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 I might be allowed to draw my own pension, but I cannot say whether it will cover the gap until the provider gives me a net figure. Payroll appeals still face 2031 AGI, and site payroll paperwork does too; physical workplace checks face robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January 2027 I’d meet with Elias and price a smaller flat on the same bus line, including the deposit and moving cost. Before 2031 we would move only if he agrees, the landlord confirms a transferable deposit and the rent saving pays back the move within a year; in the first year after AGI I’d keep applying for posted paid appeals work if my own pension and his fixed payment do not cover rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious but five years lets us see actual rents. I would not trade three weeks cash for a cheaper advert that costs more to reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the same bus line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A far-off cheaper flat could cost my remaining wage in fares. I still need to reach any posted pay job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the new landlord will not transfer the deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we stay and keep looking. I cannot put a second deposit on a card and call it a saving.

say: I’d demand a **real closure date** and written pay for any appeal post.
Workers should know whether a **human pay contact** survives the change.
think: My pension’s **net amount at 63** is not yet known.
Payroll appeals face **2031 AGI** before 2034 robots affect physical checks.
do: Price a **smaller flat** on the same bus line, including deposit and moving costs.
Move before 2031 only with **Elias’s agreement**, transferable deposit and one-year payback from rent savings.
Seek **posted paid appeals work** after AGI if combined pensions cannot cover rent and food.
feel: I feel **anxious** but can compare actual rents.
S3.quote: I cannot put a second deposit on a card and call it a saving.
fieldNote: She tests **net housing cost**, not the advertised rent alone.
The bus line and deposit are **hard move conditions** with thin cash.
She does not treat **age 63** as proof of adequate pension income.

steps.text: Price smaller flats on current bus line including deposit and moving costs
Move only with Elias’s agreement transferable deposit and rent savings repaying costs within one year
Apply after 2031 for posted paid appeals if combined pension income cannot cover rent and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our clerks a decade is time to put pension figures and staff notice dates on paper. I would still ask that every worker has a way to contest a missing payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 in 2036, and our children would still have their own households. My wage may already be gone, and Elias’s fixed pension is not enough on its own; my own pension may help, but I cannot retire on an age without a written net amount and access date. Payroll decisions face 2036 AGI, with physical workplace checks following robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From next year I’d check my provider’s pension access and net income each January and put 25 a month into rent cash only after our bills clear. By 2036 Elias and I would compare our combined verified payments with the actual smaller-flat rent and move only if the deposit, bus and one-year cost saving work; in the first year after AGI I’d take posted paid appeals work if the pensions fall short, and keep looking if no employer offers it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, even with ten years. I would welcome retirement if it paid the rent; I will not give the landlord a birthday card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop applying for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only verified money we can actually draw and live on, plus a rent we can pay. I would not stop because someone says sixty-eight sounds old enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the children to move home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have homes and jobs of their own. We may ask them for advice about a flat, but I would not make their income our retirement plan.

say: I’d put **pension figures** and staff notice dates on paper.
Workers still need a **missing-pay appeal** when AI makes decisions.
think: At **68 in 2036**, pension access and net income remain the deciding facts.
Elias’s **fixed pension** cannot cover living costs alone; payroll decisions face 2036 AGI before 2039 robots.
do: Check **pension income** and access each January; save 25 monthly only after bills clear.
Compare **verified combined income** with a cheaper flat alongside Elias; move only if deposit, bus and one-year savings work.
Take **posted paid appeals** after AGI if pensions fall short; keep searching if none is offered.
feel: I feel **anxious** because age alone cannot pay rent.
S4.quote: I will not give the landlord a birthday card.
fieldNote: Her small monthly saving follows **paid bills**, not an imagined pension.
The **existing partner pension** is known, while her own access and amount require checking.
She plans to **work at 68** if combined income cannot cover rent.

steps.text: Check provider’s written pension access and net monthly amount each January
Save 25 monthly toward rent only after household bills clear
Move only if Elias agrees, deposit transfers, bus works and one-year rent savings repay costs
Take posted paid appeals after 2036 if verified pensions fall short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a junior payroll desk is easy to close and three weeks cash is no cushion. I need written notice, my own pension figures and a reachable paid vacancy before I can plan. Elias’s pension buys groceries, not the rent and food together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who tells a worker their weekend premium was missing because we misread the signed card. I would rather make that awkward call myself than send a perfect letter with the wrong amount. A payslip is a promise about Friday, not a poem about efficiency.

headlineQuote: A payslip is a promise about Friday, not a poem about efficiency.
portrait: **Nora**, 58, is a new junior payroll manager after years at the time-clock desk.
Her bachelor’s degree does not erase **rule-learning gaps** in the new role.
Low pay, **three weeks cash** and rising rent keep her anxious even in a plateau.
Elias already receives a **small fixed pension**, while her own access and net amount are unknown.
She has **never used AI** and seeks signed cards, legal pay accuracy and actual paid work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could close her junior desk before she verifies pension income or finds another wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, her own pension figures and a reachable paid vacancy would help her plan.
